analysis.one_liner: Requires websites and apps to protect user data, use it in users' interest, and restrict sharing or selling it.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat for the rest of the Congress after being referred there in March 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Data Care Act would have imposed three legal duties on any company that collects personal data online: keep it secure, don't use it in ways that foreseeably harm the user, and don't share or sell it unless the recipient takes on the same duties. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce these rules, with penalties scaled to how long a violation lasted or how many users were harmed. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet. The bill treated personal data the way bankers treat deposited money: companies would owe users a duty of care (secure the data, tell you promptly if sensitive data like your Social Security number or health records is breached), a duty of loyalty (don't use your data in ways that benefit the company at your expense), and a duty of confidentiality (don't hand your data to anyone who hasn't accepted the same obligations). Users could not be made to sign these rights away, and violations could bring per-user civil penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Online service providers would owe users duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality: reasonably securing personal data, not using it in ways that cause foreseeable material physical or financial harm, and not disclosing or selling it except under contract terms that pass the same duties along.

Companies would have to promptly notify users of any breach involving sensitive data such as Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, biometric data, health information, precise location, or private messages.

The Federal Trade Commission could enforce violations the same way it enforces consumer protection law, including against nonprofits and phone and cable companies, and state attorneys general could sue violators for civil penalties calculated by the number of days of noncompliance or the number of users harmed.
Users could not waive or sign away these rights by contract, and any company that received user data from a provider would be bound by the same rules.

analysis.who_pays: Companies whose business models run on collecting and monetizing personal data: social media platforms, digital advertising networks, and data brokers. They would face compliance costs and lose the ability to sell or freely share user data. Some costs could be passed to users, and the bill's broad standards would have required legal judgment calls by every online business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data-driven platforms, ad networks, data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill gave individuals no right to sue on their own; only the FTC and state officials could enforce it, so relief would depend entirely on government action.

Standards like harm that is 'unexpected and highly offensive to a reasonable end user' are broad and somewhat vague, which could create legal uncertainty for ordinary online businesses and chill legitimate uses of data like fraud detection and service personalization.

Compliance costs would fall on every online business that collects any personally linkable data, though the FTC could exempt smaller or lower-risk providers after weighing the privacy risks and costs and benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the upside is substantial: a uniform federal floor for how any company handles the personal data it collects about you, with real penalties and no way to contract them away. The costs fall mainly on companies profiting from unrestricted data collection, with some risk of higher compliance burdens for small businesses that the FTC could soften through exemptions. The main design weakness is that ordinary users get no direct right to sue, leaving enforcement to the FTC and state attorneys general.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never took it up: after the bill was introduced and referred to the committee in March 2023, no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote ever happened, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the bill on March 9, 2023 with 18 original cosponsors, all Democrats or independents.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies whose business models depend on collecting and selling personal data are better off, because no federal data duties were enacted and the status quo continued. Online users gained nothing; no comparable comprehensive data privacy law passed in this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Data Care Act of 2023 on March 9, 2023.

for.name: 19 Senate cosponsors (17 Democrats, 2 independents)
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Sens. Warren, Klobuchar, Sanders, Booker, and Durbin
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors when the bill was introduced; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to and never left
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate majority was held by Democrats; Republicans controlled 49 seats and no member of the party cosponsored
against.what_they_did: No Senate Republican cosponsored the bill, and the bill never reached the floor, where bipartisan consent is typically needed to schedule most legislation.

against.name: Large online platforms and the digital advertising industry
against.role: Companies whose revenue depends on collecting and monetizing personal data
against.what_they_did: Comprehensive federal privacy legislation imposing duties on data collection stalled in Congress throughout this period, with major tech companies lobbying against strict data-handling mandates.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced beyond a Democratic-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Digital advertising and large online platforms
industries.note: These companies monetize personal data through targeted advertising; the bill's loyalty and confidentiality duties would restrict how they collect, use, and share user data and expose them to per-user penalties. Their interest in unrestricted data use runs against the bill's protections for users.

Firms that buy, sell, and trade personal information would be directly restricted: they could not receive data from providers without taking on the same duties, and violations could bring penalties scaled to users harmed.
Any business collecting linkable personal data would face compliance obligations, but the FTC could exempt smaller or lower-risk providers after weighing privacy risks against costs and benefits.

industries.industry: State attorneys general and consumer protection offices
industries.note: The bill would have handed state officials a new federal cause of action with civil penalties against data violators, expanding their enforcement toolkit alongside the FTC.
